options.label: Assert selected record
options.result: Fails when the wrong visit changes.
options.why: The check observes the actual requirement.

options.label: Count test cases
options.result: No conclusion about this defect.
options.why: Quantity is not the same as a meaningful expectation.

example.before: Tests assert the same broken calculation used by the app.
example.action: Write an expected example from the business rule and deliberately introduce a defect in a disposable test change.
example.after: The check fails, AI fixes the cause, and the original expectation passes.
example.lesson: Do not weaken the expectation just to make the suite green. AI can generate and run every check; explain why it is relevant.

project.title: Checks that can prove you wrong
project.brief: Ask AI to create appropriate unit, integration and journey checks from the acceptance matrix. Demonstrate one real defect and keep its regression check.
steps: Map important requirements to checks and expected observations.
Introduce or use a known defect in a test environment and show the relevant failure.
Let AI diagnose and fix it; rerun the focused check and affected journey, recording remaining limits.
checks: Each important check has a requirement-derived expectation and suitable test data.
A deliberate or observed defect produces a meaningful failing check.
The fix passes the original expectation and relevant regression checks without hiding the failure.

assess.explain: Explain the different evidence from unit, integration and journey checks.
assess.locate: Show the expectation that exposed your defect and its source requirement.
assess.predict: What would still pass if the wrong visit changed but the toast looked correct?
assess.compare: Compare a faster isolated check with a broader journey check.
assess.challenge: AI says all green means there are no bugs. Name an untested behaviour and how to investigate it.
assess.guide: Supply an uncovered edge case and ask the learner to choose evidence before running it.
variations: The test uses only one customer, hiding an authorization bug. Improve the data.
A mocked provider passes while its real schema changed. Choose an additional boundary check.

title: Release with a way back
problem: The app works locally but the release uses different configuration. Plan delivery and recovery together so a failed change does not become a guess under pressure.
outcome: A documented release and a demonstrated recovery in an appropriate environment.

concepts.name: Version history, builds and environments
concepts.explanation: Version history records changes and a known starting point. A build turns source and dependencies into runnable output. An environment supplies configuration, services and access. A working local setup may differ from the deployed one in any of these.
concepts.example: A release points to a specific revision and dependency configuration.
concepts.misconception: The latest files on a laptop identify exactly what users are running.

concepts.name: CI/CD, rollback and state
concepts.explanation: Continuous integration checks changes; delivery/deployment pipelines prepare or release them. Rollback restores a suitable previous application version. Stored data may need a separate restoration or compatible migration plan; reverting code does not undo every external action.
concepts.example: An older release must still understand the current data schema before it is a safe rollback.
concepts.misconception: A green pipeline proves production is healthy.

experiment.prompt: Change the release situation in this prepared model.

options.label: Build passes, secret absent
options.result: Release can still fail at runtime configuration.
options.why: Build success does not supply a missing server credential.

options.label: Code-only regression
options.result: A compatible previous release may restore the journey.
options.why: Verify the actual result after rollback.

options.label: Incompatible data migration
options.result: Code rollback alone may be unsafe or insufficient.
options.why: Stored-state compatibility needs its own recovery plan.

example.before: Deploy whatever is in the current folder.
example.action: Ask AI to release an identified revision with environment checks, smoke tests and a compatible recovery target.
example.after: A failed test release can return to a known working journey.
example.lesson: Demonstrate recovery in a test environment first. Record exact commands or provider actions through AI-generated instructions you can explain.

project.title: A release you can recover
project.brief: Release the product to a suitable test or authorized public environment with identified source, configuration and a recovery procedure.
steps: Ask AI to inspect the current stack, prepare reproducible build/release instructions and name required configuration without secrets.
Release a known revision and verify its main user journey from the deployed environment.
Introduce a reversible test failure, recover, and verify both application behaviour and required data.
checks: The running release is tied to an identified revision, build and environment.
An actual deployed user journey is observed separately from pipeline success.
A recovery demonstration restores required behaviour and accounts for stored-state compatibility.

assess.explain: Explain source, build, configuration, deployment and rollback in this release.
assess.locate: Identify the running version and where required configuration is supplied.
assess.predict: What might fail when local dependencies differ from the release environment?
assess.compare: Compare reverting code with restoring data and reconciling external effects.
assess.challenge: AI says the green pipeline proves the site works for users. What observation is missing?
assess.guide: Change one environment variable or version in a test scenario and ask for a bounded investigation and recovery.
variations: The previous code cannot read the new schema. Revise recovery.
The build succeeds but a server configuration value is missing. Trace the failure.

title: Diagnose from evidence
problem: Some confirmations are slow and others fail. Instead of asking AI to randomly rewrite the feature, collect evidence that distinguishes possible causes.
outcome: An incident investigation with a tested hypothesis and verified recovery.

concepts.name: Logs, metrics and traces
concepts.explanation: Logs record events, metrics summarize measurements, and traces connect steps of a request. Correlation identifiers help follow one action across components. Instrumentation should avoid secrets and unnecessary personal information.
concepts.example: A request ID connects the browser error, API event and slow provider call.
concepts.misconception: More raw logging automatically makes diagnosis easier or safer.

concepts.name: Hypotheses and falsification
concepts.explanation: A hypothesis is a possible explanation with a predicted observation. Choose evidence that can distinguish it from another explanation. AI can investigate and propose fixes; verify the actual user flow after change rather than treating a convincing diagnosis as the result.
concepts.example: If the provider is slow, its span should dominate latency while local validation remains fast.
concepts.misconception: The first plausible explanation is the established cause.

experiment.prompt: Prepared trace: total 2,000 ms; validation 20 ms; database 80 ms; provider 1,900 ms. Choose an investigation.

options.label: Rewrite CSS
options.result: No evidence links styling to the measured server delay.
options.why: Choose a hypothesis connected to the observed boundary.

options.label: Inspect provider span
options.result: A relevant next step: check its timing, errors and comparison requests.
options.why: The trace identifies a candidate; it does not yet explain why the provider is slow.

options.label: Declare cause solved
options.result: Premature: no corrective change or recovered journey observed.
options.why: Diagnosis and verified recovery are different outcomes.

example.before: A user reports slow saves; AI suggests a database rewrite.
example.action: Collect a correlated trace and compare a provider-delay hypothesis with a database-delay hypothesis.
example.after: Evidence directs a bounded change, followed by a timed user journey.
example.lesson: Record contradictory evidence and remaining uncertainty. Do not expose private notes in diagnostic artifacts.

project.title: An evidence-led incident record
project.brief: Instrument and investigate one real or deliberately injected test failure using AI, with privacy-aware observations and a verified fix.
steps: Define the symptom, environment and two plausible hypotheses.
Ask AI to collect appropriately redacted logs, metrics or traces that distinguish them.
Apply a bounded fix, rerun the relevant flow and record cause, evidence, recovery and remaining risks.
checks: The incident record separates symptom, hypothesis and observed evidence.
A correlated observation supports or refutes a hypothesis without leaking credentials or private data.
The relevant user journey works after the fix and its observed result is recorded.

assess.explain: Explain a log, metric, trace and hypothesis through this incident.
assess.locate: Find the observation that changed the investigation's direction.
assess.predict: What would you expect to see if the database were the bottleneck instead?
assess.compare: Compare collecting all payloads with targeted privacy-aware instrumentation.
assess.challenge: AI says the last changed file must be the cause. Propose a distinguishing investigation.
assess.guide: Provide contradictory evidence and see whether the learner revises the explanation rather than defending the first guess.
variations: Only one region experiences failures. Refine the hypotheses.
Logs contain a credential. Explain the immediate handling and instrumentation change.

title: Manage growing use and cost
problem: The system feels slow as appointments grow. Caching, indexing and queues solve different problems and introduce tradeoffs. Measure before choosing.
outcome: A measured bottleneck improvement with cost and correctness limits.

concepts.name: Latency, throughput and algorithmic cost
concepts.explanation: Latency is time per operation; throughput is completed work per time. A data structure organizes information and affects available operations. Algorithmic cost describes how work grows with input size. An index can speed a query while adding storage and write cost.
concepts.example: Scanning every visit grows differently from a suitable indexed lookup.
concepts.misconception: A faster one-user response proves the system handles more simultaneous users.

concepts.name: Caching, queues and consistency
concepts.explanation: A cache reuses a result and can become stale. A queue defers work and needs failure and retry rules. Consistency concerns when different observations agree. Choose freshness and delay according to the business task, not just a benchmark.
concepts.example: A cached policy may tolerate a refresh delay; a last-slot reservation needs a protected current decision.
concepts.misconception: Caching every response preserves correct behaviour automatically.

experiment.prompt: Change the prepared design for repeated policy reads.

options.label: Always fetch current
options.result: Freshness follows the source; each read pays the source latency and cost.
options.why: This favours current information over reuse.

options.label: Cache for 10 minutes
options.result: Repeated reads may be faster but can show a policy up to the freshness limit out of date.
options.why: Invalidation and an accepted freshness policy are part of the design.

options.label: Queue the read
options.result: Work is deferred; this alone does not make an interactive answer faster.
options.why: Queues fit suitable background tasks, not every delay.

example.before: A broad scan gets slower as the visit table grows.
example.action: Measure representative queries, ask AI to propose an index, and compare the same workload afterwards.
example.after: Report read improvement, write/storage effects and limitations of the test load.
example.lesson: Synthetic measurements establish behaviour under the stated test conditions, not unlimited production capacity.

project.title: One measured performance improvement
project.brief: Identify one actual bottleneck in the growing workflow, compare an appropriate improvement and report correctness, cost and measurement limits.
steps: Define representative load, latency/throughput measures and a correctness guardrail.
Let AI measure the current system and propose indexing, data-structure, cache or queue changes as appropriate.
Rerun the same workload and user journey; record improvement, resource cost and freshness/retry consequences.
checks: Before and after measurements use comparable data, workload and environment.
The change improves the chosen measure or is honestly rejected from the results.
Correctness, freshness or retry behaviour remains acceptable and added cost is recorded.

assess.explain: Explain latency, throughput, workload growth and the selected mechanism.
assess.locate: Find the measured bottleneck and actual boundary changed.
assess.predict: What changes as record count or concurrent demand increases?
assess.compare: Compare two plausible interventions with cost and consistency tradeoffs.
assess.challenge: AI says a 10-minute cache always gives current availability. Show the counterexample and a suitable policy.
assess.guide: Change load or freshness needs; ask the learner to revisit the design rather than recite a speed figure.
variations: The cached data now determines the last available slot. Reconsider correctness.
The queue receives work faster than it can finish. Predict backlog and recovery needs.

title: Change the system without losing trust
problem: A new visit field and a dependency update are needed. The running system contains useful records, permissions and deletion commitments that must survive the change.
outcome: A rehearsed migration or dependency change with restoration evidence.

concepts.name: Migrations, backups and restoration
concepts.explanation: A migration changes stored structure or data. A backup is a recoverable copy under a defined scope. Restoration is the act of rebuilding usable state from that copy. A backup is not proven usable until a relevant restore has been checked.
concepts.example: Add an access-status field without silently converting unknown values into confirmed.
concepts.misconception: Reverting source code automatically reverses a data migration.

concepts.name: Compatibility, privacy and retention
concepts.explanation: Dependency versions and data formats define compatibility. Privacy includes what is collected, who can access it, how long it is retained and how deletion reaches relevant copies. A restore plan must consider permissions and data commitments, not just row counts.
concepts.example: A restored copy should not re-enable a deleted user's access.
concepts.misconception: A backup can be kept forever without any data responsibility.

experiment.prompt: Choose the prepared recovery evidence.

options.label: Backup file exists
options.result: A copy exists; usability is unverified.
options.why: The file may be incomplete, inaccessible or incompatible.

options.label: Restored and queried
options.result: Relevant state can be read; check permissions and required journeys too.
options.why: Restoration evidence should match what the product depends on.

options.label: Only code reverted
options.result: Stored data and external effects may remain changed.
options.why: Application history and data history are different boundaries.

example.before: A migration maps every blank access value to confirmed.
example.action: Ask AI to rehearse on a copy, preserve unknown meaning, compare records and test restoration.
example.after: The new version preserves information meaning and has an observed recovery path.
example.lesson: Protect fictional test copies appropriately too. Never treat a production data change as disposable practice.

project.title: A change with a recovery rehearsal
project.brief: Use AI to perform a data migration or dependency update in a test copy. Verify required data, permissions and behaviour, and demonstrate restoration.
steps: Record compatibility, data meaning, retention commitments and recovery scope before the change.
Create a suitable test copy and let AI rehearse the change and relevant checks.
Restore from the recovery copy, verify the main flow and record what the rehearsal does and does not establish.
checks: Important record counts, relationships and meanings are compared before and after.
Required permissions and privacy/retention decisions survive or have an explicit migration policy.
A restoration is actually demonstrated and the required user journey is verified afterwards.

assess.explain: Explain migration, backup, restoration and compatibility in your change.
assess.locate: Find the actual stored format, dependency version and recovery copy.
assess.predict: What if an older app reads the newly migrated data?
assess.compare: Compare rollback, forward correction and restoring a backup for this situation.
assess.challenge: AI says a backup's filename proves recoverability. What demonstration is needed?
assess.guide: Ask about a missing record, revoked permission or incompatible reader after recovery; check the explanation concerns the actual system.
variations: A restored copy contains a previously deleted account. Revise recovery handling.
The new dependency changes a default used by the API. Investigate compatibility.

title: Start an independent domain project
problem: Transfer the concepts to an unfamiliar workflow: building maintenance, a clinic's non-clinical administration, logistics, education or another authorized domain. A familiar demo is not evidence that you understand this setting.
outcome: A domain-grounded project brief with a discovered requirement and measurement plan.

concepts.name: Domain constraints and incentives
concepts.explanation: Domain knowledge explains the real work and its limits. Incentives explain why people may adopt, avoid or work around a change. The person requesting the app may not be the person doing the extra work. Investigate both perspectives.
concepts.example: A manager wants more completed visits; technicians need travel and access time counted fairly.
concepts.misconception: A reusable app template establishes the requirements of every business.

concepts.name: Success agreement and uncertainty
concepts.explanation: A brief records the problem, source evidence, scope, authority, constraints and success conditions. Uncertainty belongs in the brief as questions and assumptions. AI can research and prepare it, but invented details must stay labelled.
concepts.example: Separate an observed missed handoff from a guess about its annual cost.
concepts.misconception: A detailed AI-written proposal makes an unverified workflow factual.

experiment.prompt: Choose what you discover during a maintenance-workflow investigation.

options.label: Manager wants faster dispatch
options.result: A goal to examine with the people doing the work.
options.why: Speed may conflict with equipment, travel or access constraints.

options.label: Technician lacks access approval
options.result: A missing requirement that changes the workflow and acceptance criteria.
options.why: A new scheduling screen alone would not resolve the blockage.

options.label: AI estimates savings
options.result: A hypothesis requiring assumptions and measurements.
options.why: Generated numbers are not observed business benefit.

example.before: Reuse the appointment app unchanged in a building-maintenance company.
example.action: Investigate a recent visit and discover site-access approval and equipment qualifications.
example.after: The brief changes the allowed assignments and definition of a preventable missed visit.
example.lesson: The concepts transfer; the domain assumptions require fresh evidence.

project.title: An independent outcome brief
project.brief: Investigate an unfamiliar authorized domain and define a useful improvement with participants or a clearly labelled scenario. Include local language, connectivity, cost and data constraints.
steps: Choose the domain, access boundary and evidence sources; use AI for research and questions.
Map the workflow, incentives and a requirement missing from the initial request.
Compare buy/configure/integrate/build options and agree or label success, scope and measurement assumptions.
checks: The brief identifies sources, users, incentives and at least one discovered requirement.
Success, scope, authority and constraints are explicit without invented measurement.
An alternative approach and a plan to measure actual benefit are documented.

assess.explain: Explain what domain understanding changed in your initial idea.
assess.locate: Find the source behind the discovered requirement and an important unknown.
assess.predict: What if the person entering data gains extra work but no benefit?
assess.compare: Compare the selected approach with buying or configuring an existing product.
assess.challenge: AI says an old demo proves this workflow's business case. What fresh evidence is needed?
assess.guide: Introduce a plausible domain constraint omitted from the brief and ask the learner to revise scope and success.
variations: The workflow must support low connectivity and two languages. Revise the brief.
The measured delay includes customer cancellations. Reassess the outcome definition.

title: Deliver through AI
problem: Deliver the independent brief with the AI available to you. A polished artifact must be accompanied by an accurate explanation of its actual stack, information flow and decisions.
outcome: A working solution and a maintained system explanation tied to real observations.

concepts.name: Architecture as responsibilities and tradeoffs
concepts.explanation: Architecture describes responsibilities, boundaries and dependencies. Coupling is how strongly one part depends on another. Modularity can make change easier, but extra services also add operations and failure boundaries. Choose complexity proportionate to the outcome.
concepts.example: One application may fit a small workflow better than several separately deployed services.
concepts.misconception: More layers always mean more professional architecture.

concepts.name: Evidence-linked delivery
concepts.explanation: Delivery combines implementation, checks, configuration, access and a usable result. AI may perform the whole technical sequence. Keep the system explanation synchronized with meaningful changes and distinguish actual observations from planned checks.
concepts.example: A claimed enquiry feature needs evidence that the enquiry reaches the chosen destination.
concepts.misconception: A generated system description is accurate because the app looks complete.

experiment.prompt: Change the prepared architecture for a small information-only service.

options.label: Static site fits the need
options.result: Explain files, browser behaviour and hosting. No invented backend is needed.
options.why: The explanation must match the actual product's responsibilities.

options.label: Needs shared private records
options.result: Add suitable storage, identity and trusted permission boundaries.
options.why: The requirement adds responsibilities beyond a static page.

options.label: Add many services anyway
options.result: More configuration and failure boundaries without an established benefit.
options.why: Complexity needs a reason connected to constraints.

example.before: The diagram shows a database and model service copied from a template.
example.action: Inspect the actual project with AI and trace a real action from start to result.
example.after: The diagram contains only implemented components, with planned extensions labelled.
example.lesson: A static solution can be correct. A backend solution needs deeper data, access and failure evidence as those responsibilities appear.

project.title: The independent working solution
project.brief: Use capable AI to deliver the mission-26 brief. Choose suitable technologies, implement the useful workflow and maintain an accurate explanation throughout.
steps: Supply AI the domain evidence, acceptance matrix, authority and budget; let it plan appropriate work.
Deliver in useful increments, inspect actual technologies and update all eight system-explanation areas.
Demonstrate the main journey, a relevant failure and any permission/data boundaries; record gaps honestly.
checks: The actual product demonstrates the brief's primary useful outcome.
Checks cover relevant normal, failure and access/data cases with reproducible observations.
The system explanation matches the real files, dependencies, runtime, hosting and information flow.

assess.explain: Explain the architecture and how its boundaries serve the outcome.
assess.locate: Identify every important technology in actual files, configuration or service settings.
assess.predict: Choose one failed component and predict what the user and stored state would show.
assess.compare: Defend an important technology choice against a simpler or more portable alternative.
assess.challenge: AI's diagram includes an unused service. Explain how to verify and correct the description.
assess.guide: Choose an action from the live product, trace its real path and ask a new requirement question with AI available.
variations: The budget is cut while the outcome stays the same. Revise architecture or scope.
A key provider becomes unavailable. Explain a proportionate alternative.

title: Respond to reality
problem: The product works technically, but staff avoid it. Learn whether it improves the whole workflow, causes extra work elsewhere or misses a practical constraint.
outcome: An observed feedback cycle, a changed requirement and a bounded benefit claim.

concepts.name: Adoption, training and downstream effects
concepts.explanation: Adoption means people can and choose to use the result in their work. Training, trust, time and incentives affect it. A faster step can move a bottleneck or increase another person's workload. Observe the whole journey, not just the new screen.
concepts.example: Dispatch saves time while technicians spend longer correcting incomplete access details.
concepts.misconception: A successful deployment proves useful adoption.

concepts.name: Feedback, maintenance and causal limits
concepts.explanation: Feedback is evidence about experience and outcomes, with a source and context. Maintenance includes correcting defects and adapting to changed conditions. Compare outcomes carefully: selection, seasonality and other changes can explain a before/after difference.
concepts.example: Report a small pilot's observed rate without claiming it proves the app caused every improvement.
concepts.misconception: Positive comments alone establish financial benefit.

experiment.prompt: The prepared pilot reduces dispatch time by 10 minutes per day. Change what happens downstream.

options.label: No extra downstream work
options.result: A candidate improvement, subject to measurement and sample limits.
options.why: Still check data quality and other changes before a causal claim.

options.label: 20 extra minutes correcting visits
options.result: The local speedup may worsen total workflow effort.
options.why: Evaluate the whole outcome rather than the favoured step.

options.label: Staff do not use it
options.result: Investigate access, fit, training and incentives before claiming impact.
options.why: Technical availability and adoption differ.

example.before: The dashboard is live, but staff keep a separate spreadsheet.
example.action: Observe the task, discover missing offline access and compare total workflow effort.
example.after: Adapt the product and training, then repeat a bounded pilot.
example.lesson: Clearly label scenario feedback when real participants are unavailable. Do not invent customers or benefit measurements.

project.title: An improvement tested in use
project.brief: Run an authorized pilot or clearly labelled scenario trial of the independent solution. Investigate adoption and a changed requirement, then improve and remeasure.
steps: Define the pilot participants, consent, outcome measure and guardrails.
Observe use and capture specific confusion, extra work and a changed constraint.
Delegate a suitable improvement to AI, update the system explanation and repeat the relevant task and measurement.
checks: Feedback and outcome observations have sources and an honest real/scenario label.
A changed requirement leads to a justified product or process improvement.
The benefit statement includes downstream effects, uncertainty and remaining adoption gaps.

assess.explain: Explain the difference between deployment, adoption and demonstrated benefit.
assess.locate: Show evidence for a changed requirement and its resulting decision.
assess.predict: What if the faster workflow transfers work to another person?
assess.compare: Compare a training change with a software change for the observed confusion.
assess.challenge: AI says happier pilot users prove the product caused a 20% business improvement. What evidence is missing?
assess.guide: Offer contradictory pilot feedback or a different denominator and ask the learner to revise the conclusion.
variations: The most active users are also the most experienced staff. Reassess the comparison.
The product meets its target but creates extra work for customers. Revise the guardrail.

title: Transfer the work and adapt
problem: Another person must operate the product without relying on your memory. The current AI tool or provider may also become unsuitable. Preserve the useful outcome while changing how it is delivered.
outcome: A usable handoff and a demonstrated transfer to an unfamiliar tool or changed constraint.

concepts.name: Handoff, ownership and runbooks
concepts.explanation: A handoff transfers the knowledge, access and responsibility needed to operate the result. A runbook describes observable symptoms and appropriate actions. Name ownership, escalation and maintenance decisions. Documentation must match the current product and avoid embedding secrets.
concepts.example: A new operator can start the service, verify a visit and follow recovery instructions.
concepts.misconception: A long README proves another person can run the product.

concepts.name: Portability and conceptual transfer
concepts.explanation: Portability concerns moving data and behaviour across tools, services or environments. Conceptual transfer means applying a mental model in an unfamiliar setting. An adapter can isolate provider-specific details, but formats, policy and operational differences still need checks.
concepts.example: Replace an AI provider while preserving the output contract and rerunning the same evaluation.
concepts.misconception: Changing a model name guarantees equivalent behaviour and cost.

experiment.prompt: Choose what the prepared handoff includes.

options.label: Source files only
options.result: Setup, configuration, ownership and recovery may remain unknown.
options.why: Implementation alone does not transfer operational knowledge.

options.label: Guide + fresh operator trial
options.result: Observed confusion can reveal missing instructions and assumptions.
options.why: The handoff is evaluated by someone completing the task.

options.label: Provider swapped, no checks
options.result: Compatibility and quality remain unverified.
options.why: A stable interface does not guarantee equivalent semantics or economics.

example.before: Only the original builder knows the hidden configuration.
example.action: Ask AI to draft a current setup/runbook and have another person or a fresh-context assistant follow it, labelling which was used.
example.after: Fix missing steps and rerun the journey with a replacement component or unfamiliar environment.
example.lesson: A fresh-context AI trial is useful evidence about instructions; it is not evidence that a human operator adopted the product.

project.title: A handoff that survives change
project.brief: Transfer the independent solution to another operator and adapt one tool, provider or environment while preserving required outcomes.
steps: Prepare a current diagram, setup guide, configuration names, cost/ownership notes, data export and recovery runbook.
Observe a new operator or labelled fresh-context trial and repair instruction gaps.

Ownership, configuration, cost, data handling and recovery instructions match the actual product without secrets.

assess.compare: Compare an adapter change with a full rebuild for your portability need.

title: Demonstrate professional capability
problem: Present useful work and explain it under a fresh condition. The final challenge tests concepts and delivery with AI available, not memorized syntax or a polished presentation alone.
outcome: An evidence-based capability review, an adapted product and an honest next-practice plan.

concepts.name: Demonstration and fresh-scenario reasoning
concepts.explanation: A demonstration connects a claim to an observable result. A fresh scenario changes a requirement or failure condition to test whether a mental model transfers. AI remains available; the learner must apply the concepts, make predictions and explain evidence rather than repeat a prepared script.
concepts.example: Explain the real stack, then adapt when a provider is unavailable or a client changes the goal.
concepts.misconception: Course completion automatically equals years of professional employment.

concepts.name: Capability, uncertainty and adaptation
concepts.explanation: Capability is demonstrated responsibility under stated conditions. Record help, decisions, time, costs, gaps and review. Future opportunities depend on technology, adoption and institutions. Planning and coordination may also be automated; keep learning and compare outcomes with comparable tools.
concepts.example: A reviewer records which concepts transferred and which need another demonstration.
concepts.misconception: A new job title guarantees a permanently protected career.

options.why: Ask the learner to explain actual technologies and respond to a fresh change.

options.result: Relevant capability evidence under the stated tools and review conditions.
options.why: Record limits honestly; it is not an employment guarantee or authenticated credential.

example.before: A learner presents an impressive system but cannot say where its records live.
example.action: Revisit storage with an experiment, then ask for a new prediction and trace in their actual product.
example.after: Record demonstrated reasoning or a specific gap needing further practice.
example.lesson: Useful AI output and learner understanding are separate standards. Manual coding is not required to meet either standard.

project.title: The independent delivery challenge
project.brief: Investigate an unfamiliar business problem, use available AI to improve it, explain the actual technologies and concepts, demonstrate benefit, and adapt when conditions change.
steps: Assemble the independent product, eight-part system explanation, evidence, costs, feedback and honest contribution record.
Ask a reviewer to select a fresh requirement or failure relevant to the product; predict its effects, then use AI to adapt and verify.
Review the shared foundation, record demonstrated areas and gaps, and choose further practice. Compare with experienced participants only using actual comparable task/tool evidence.
checks: The demonstrated product addresses an evidenced or explicitly labelled scenario problem with proportionate outcome checks.
The learner explains the actual stack, runtime, action flow, data, authority, choices and failure behaviour.
A fresh condition is investigated and handled with AI available; the review records observed reasoning, limits and next practice.

assess.explain: Explain the purpose, system and important decisions without relying on a prepared script.
assess.locate: Trace one reviewer-chosen action through the actual technologies and evidence.
assess.predict: Predict an unfamiliar requirement or failure before asking AI to implement the response.
assess.compare: Defend an important choice when cost, access or the business goal changes.
assess.challenge: AI claims completion proves the equivalent of five years' experience. Explain why the evidence supports only the demonstrated capabilities.
assess.guide: Review all eight system areas and five reasoning actions. Use a fresh relevant scenario, observe the reasoning and actual result, and record gaps. This local review record is not an authenticated qualification.
variations: The client's goal changes, the dataset is misleading and a provider becomes unsuitable. Choose a relevant combination and adapt with evidence.
A convincing request lacks verified authority. Explain and demonstrate how the system handles it without losing the legitimate workflow.
